Title: Google Business Profile Automation: The Complete Guide for Local Businesses

URL Source: https://dmly.io/google-business-profile-automation-guide/

Published Time: 2026-08-13T10:58:01+00:00

Markdown Content:
Your Google Business Profile may be one of the first things people see when they search for your business. But keeping it active means checking reviews, replying to customers, updating information, and remembering to ask happy customers for feedback.

For a busy local business, those little tasks pile up fast.

But with Google Business Profile automation, you can take much of that repetitive work off your plate. You can automatically request reviews after customer visits, keep track of new feedback, manage your profile, and use AI to help with responses.

In this guide, we’ll look at what you can automate, what you should still handle personally, and how to build a system that keeps your Google presence working even when you’re busy elsewhere.

## **What Is Google Business Profile Automation?**

Google Business Profile automation, also known as GBP automation, is the use of software and automated workflows to handle repetitive tasks involved in managing your business presence on Google.

Instead of remembering to check your profile and perform every action manually, you can set up certain tasks to happen automatically when something triggers them.

Take reviews as an example. Normally, your receptionist might finish an appointment, remember to message the customer later, find your [Google review link](https://dmly.io/google-review-link/), and send it manually. With automation, completing the appointment can trigger the review request for you.

The same idea can apply to other parts of profile and reputation management. Depending on the software you use, you can:

*   Send automated Google review requests after customer visits
*   Monitor new reviews without constantly checking Google
*   Get notified when customers leave feedback
*   Draft review responses with AI
*   Manage business information and opening hours
*   Publish and manage Google Business Profile posts
*   Manage several business locations from one place

The important word here is **automation**. You’re deciding beforehand what should happen when a particular event occurs.

For example:

**Appointment completed → wait 2 hours → send customer a WhatsApp review request → customer opens your Google review link → new review appears → team is notified → AI helps draft the response**

## **What Parts of a Google Business Profile Can You Automate?**

**Start with the shape of it, because the boundary is sharper than most articles on this subject admit.** A connected Google Business Profile gives you five tabs and no more: Performance, Reviews, Request reviews, Posts and Business info. If a job is not one of those five, it is still a job you do on Google.

![Image 1: A filing drawer with five labelled tabs and two panels beside it. The tabs are the five Reputation tabs: Posts, Business info and Performance marked in green as this page's subject, and Reviews and Request reviews marked in amber and labelled as the review guide's. The first panel separates what can be edited here, phone, website, description and opening hours, from what is read-only, business name, category and address. The second panel, in red, lists three things that are not in the drawer at all: questions and answers on your listing, messaging of any kind, and replying twice to the same review. A footer warns that every Reputation tab shows made-up sample data until a profile is connected.](https://dmly.io/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/what-a-connected-google-business-profile-actually-covers.png)

**Figure 1.** Five tabs, two of which are the review guide’s subject. The panel on the right is the part worth reading twice.

Three absences are worth stating plainly, because assuming any of them costs you a morning.

**Questions and answers on your listing are not managed here.** The Q&A section that appears under a Google listing is not one of the five tabs, so answering a question a customer has posted is something you do on Google. It is worth doing: a good Q&A section answers the queries that would otherwise become phone calls. It is just not a thing you can automate from outside.

**It is not a messaging channel.** No chats, no broadcasts, no bot. A review is the only conversation Google gives you here, and the customer cannot reply to your reply. If you want to actually talk to the people leaving reviews, that happens on [a channel that carries messages](https://dmly.io/whatsapp-broadcasts-for-businesses-guide/).

**Photos reach your listing through a post, not through a photo manager.** You can attach one to an update, an offer or an event. There is no gallery to curate from here, so the photos on your listing stay Google’s business.

### **The numbers you see before you connect are not yours**

Worth knowing on day one. Every Reputation tab works before a profile is attached, and what it shows is **sample data**: made-up reviews, made-up names, made-up numbers, with a badge and a prompt saying so. It is there to show you the shape of the thing. It is not hard to mistake for your own listing on a Monday morning, and people do.

Quite a bit of the day-to-day work around your Google Business Profile can be automated or managed through one central system. The trick is knowing which tasks are repetitive enough to hand over and which ones still deserve your attention.

Here are some of the most useful areas to consider.

### **Review Requests**

This is probably the biggest opportunity for local businesses.

Instead of relying on staff to remember to ask every happy customer for a review, you can make the request part of your normal customer journey. For example, DMly can trigger a review request after an appointment and send it through WhatsApp or SMS, with a direct link to your Google review page.

A spa could automatically contact a customer a few hours after their treatment. A dentist could send the request following a completed appointment. The customer gets an easy way to leave feedback while the experience is still fresh.

### **Review Monitoring and Responses**

You shouldn’t have to open your Google Business Profile every morning just to see if somebody left a review overnight.

Review management software can bring new reviews into a central dashboard and alert your team when something needs attention. Google also provides API functionality that allows approved applications to retrieve reviews and publish replies.

AI can help with the writing too. Instead of starting every response from scratch, it can prepare a reply based on the review and your business tone.

### **Business Information**

Customers rely on Google for basics such as your address, phone number, website and opening hours.

Some Google Business Profile management platforms let you manage this information centrally rather than jumping between listings. This becomes especially useful when you have several locations.

If your restaurant group has five branches, for example, your team can manage location information through a central system instead of treating every profile as a completely separate job.

### **Opening and Special Hours**

Few things annoy customers faster than driving somewhere Google says is open, only to find the doors locked.

Regular opening hours can be managed centrally, while special hours can be prepared for holidays, temporary closures, and other changes. This is one area where automation and scheduling can reduce last-minute scrambling, although unusual changes are worth checking manually before they go live.

### **Google Posts**

Google Business Profile posts give you another place to share updates, offers, events, and news with people who find your business through Google.

Rather than remembering to create and publish each update manually, supported management tools can make planning and publishing profile content easier. This is particularly useful for businesses that already schedule content elsewhere and want Google to be part of the routine.

## **The Review Half, and Where It Is Written Up**

Two of Reputation’s five tabs are about reviews: reading them and replying, and asking for them. They are the half most people arrive looking for, and they have enough in them to fill a guide of their own, which is where they live rather than here.

The short version, so you know what you are choosing between. Reviews sync in from Google and land in your inbox as their own conversations, and you post the public owner reply from there. Review requests go out as a tracked link on WhatsApp, SMS or email, by hand from the Request reviews tab or automatically from a flow after an appointment or a payment. Two details catch people out: **a review has exactly one owner reply**, so replying again replaces what you posted rather than adding to it, and **you cannot message a reviewer**. Title: 15 Hair Salon Advertising Ideas to Get More Clients (2026)

URL Source: https://rozhair.com/blogs/education/hair-salon-advertising-ideas?srsltid=AYCX9vIdNXXuxGV-rKdglolA2QOQJbEGs8irFigzpePpcaBIjnjcFKs6

Published Time: 2026-09-01T15:19:47-0700

Markdown Content:
**If you want more clients, do not try every salon advertising idea at once.** Pick one service you want to book more often, choose one way to reach someone nearby who wants that service and make the next step easy.

For most salons, the best starting combination is simple: show up clearly on Google, display recent work that matches the service and send people to a booking page that works well on a phone. Paid ads can help you reach more people, but they work better when that foundation is already in place.

This guide explains 15 practical hair salon advertising ideas in plain English. Each one includes what it is, who it suits, what to do this week and how to tell whether it led to appointments.

I have reviewed the local-search setup of more than 300 salons that stock RŌZ. The encouraging pattern is that many missed opportunities are not technical SEO problems. They are basic pieces of information that are missing, inconsistent or hard to act on. In many cases, a salon owner can begin correcting them in about ten minutes.

## What are the best hair salon advertising ideas?

If your time and budget are limited, start with these three:

1.   **Improve your Google Business Profile** so nearby clients can understand your salon and reach your booking page.
2.   **Show the exact services you want to book** through recent photos, clear service descriptions and an easy booking path.
3.   **Ask satisfied clients for honest Google reviews** using Google’s review link or QR code.

These steps strengthen the path people already take when looking for a stylist. Once that path is clear, test one paid or promotional idea at a time.

If terms such as SEO or Google Business Profile are new to you, begin with our [plain-English guide to how new salon clients find you online](https://rozhair.com/blogs/education/hair-salon-marketing-how-new-clients-find-you-online).

## Compare the 15 ideas before you choose

| Idea | Typical cost | Time needed | Best for | What to measure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Google Business Profile | Free | Low | Local discovery | Calls, booking clicks, direction requests |
| Google reviews | Free | Low | Building trust | Review requests and new reviews |
| Service-and-location pages | Low to medium | Medium | Specialty services | Visits and bookings by page |
| Before-and-after portfolio | Free to low | Medium | Visual proof | Profile visits and booking-page clicks |
| Google Search Ads | Paid | Medium | People actively searching | Consultation requests and booked appointments |
| Instagram and Facebook ads | Paid | Medium | Visual discovery | Service-page visits and bookings |
| Follow-up ads for recent visitors | Paid | Medium | Warm website visitors | Return visits and bookings |
| Transformation videos | Free to paid | Medium | Showing a process and result | Profile visits, inquiries and bookings |
| Referral program | Offer cost | Low | Word of mouth | Referred new clients |
| Local partnerships | Free to low | Medium | Shared local audiences | Referral codes or partner bookings |
| New-client offer | Offer cost | Low | Reducing first-visit hesitation | Redemptions and second bookings |
| Last-minute opening campaign | Free to low | Low | Filling cancellations | Openings filled |
| Bridal and event campaign | Low to paid | Medium | Higher-consideration bookings | Relevant consultations |
| Neighborhood event | Low to medium | High | Local awareness | Attendees, consultations and bookings |
| Client reactivation | Free to low | Low | Past clients | Replies and returning bookings |

_Cost and effort vary by salon, market and tools. Treat this table as a way to compare options, not as a performance promise._

## Free and low-cost salon advertising ideas

### 1. Make your Google Business Profile easy to understand

Your Google Business Profile is the salon information people see in Google Search and Maps. A future client should quickly understand where you are, which services you offer, what your work looks like and how to book.

Google Ads keyword data captured in April 2026 estimated about **1.5 million U.S. searches per month for “hair salon near me”** and **110,000 per month for “hair stylist near me.”** Google groups many similar searches together, so those figures should not be added to every close variation. The practical point is simpler: a large number of people already use Google to choose a nearby salon or stylist.

#### What I found after reviewing more than 300 salon profiles

When I audited salons that stock RŌZ, the same fixable gaps appeared again and again:

*   **Services were missing.** The salon offered color, cuts or extensions, but those services were not listed on its Google profile.
*   **Important details did not match.** Hours, phone numbers, service names or other information differed between Google, the salon website and the booking page.
*   **The booking link was absent or hard to find.** A future client could discover the salon but could not move directly to an appointment.
*   **Recent work lived only on Instagram.** The salon regularly shared strong photos socially but left its Google profile looking incomplete or out of date.

These are not advanced technical problems. You do not need to begin by hiring an SEO agency. You need access to the profile, accurate information and a few focused minutes.

**Try this ten-minute check:** Open your profile as a potential client would. Confirm your real business name, address or service area, hours, phone number, categories, services and booking link. Then add a small set of recent, permission-cleared photos that represent the work you want more of. If you already create images for Instagram, reuse the appropriate ones on Google instead of creating a second content system.

Keeping the profile current gives clients better information to evaluate your salon. Google does not say that posting every day guarantees a ranking increase, so treat posts and photos as useful customer information—not a ranking trick.

**Measure:** Record calls, booking-link clicks, direction requests and completed new-client bookings. [Google says local results are mainly based on relevance, distance and prominence](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7091?hl=en); there is no way to request or pay Google for a better local position.

### 2. Ask satisfied clients for honest Google reviews

Reviews help a future client understand what it may be like to visit your salon. Ask after a completed appointment, when the experience is still fresh.

**Sample message:** “Thank you for coming in today. If you have a minute, would you share an honest Google review about your experience? Here is the link: [review link].”

**What to do this week:** Create your [official Google review link or QR code](https://support.google.com/business/answer/3474122?hl=en). Give your team one natural sentence they can use. Do not offer a reward for a positive review or tell the client what to write.

**Measure:** Review requests sent, new reviews received and whether reviews mention the services you actually provide.

### 3. Build one clear page for one important service

A single page called “Services” often asks a new client to do too much work. If balayage, curly cuts, extensions or another specialty matters to your business, give that service a page of its own.

**What the page should answer:** Who is the service for? What happens during the appointment? What may affect the price or timing? What does upkeep involve? Where is the salon? How does someone book the right appointment?

**What to do this week:** Choose one priority service and improve that page before creating five more. Use the same truthful service language on your website, Google profile and booking menu.

**Measure:** Visits to the page, clicks into booking and completed bookings for that service.

### 4. Turn recent work into a useful portfolio

A good portfolio is not simply a grid of beautiful hair. It helps a future client recognize the result they want and understand that your salon performs that service.

**What to show:** Include the finished look, useful context and the service name. If permission allows, show different starting points, hair types and finishes instead of repeating one look.

**Sample caption:** “Soft dimensional brunette by [stylist] in [neighborhood]. New color clients can begin with a consultation.”

**Measure:** Profile visits, service-page visits, consultation requests and bookings—not only likes.

Google Business Profile

Why service brands need Google Business Profile discipline, location pages, reviews, citations, and source tracking for AI recommendations.

![Image 1: Dylan Allen-Arnegard, CEO and Co-Founder of Cheers](https://www.cheers.tech/_next/image?url=%2Fimages%2Fauthors%2Fdylan-allen-arnegard.webp&w=3840&q=75&dpl=dpl_BUHf3JVNo5aAPDqXGngMbjR3Ct5T)

Google Search Central says local businesses should keep Business Profile information current for AI search, but it also says AI features rely on normal Search foundations. That guidance was updated July 10, 2026.

**Last verified: September 2, 2026.**

Google's documentation says:

> Don't just recycle what others on the internet have already said, or could easily be produced by a generative AI model.

Local AI citation mix

The profile needs an owned source stack

The Google Business Profile anchors Google identity. The much larger owned-site citation share shows why location and service pages still matter.

Cheers Market Baseline, 28 days ending September 2, 2026; 100 metros, four engines, 49,677 runs, 356,019 citations, aggregate only (corrected September 23, 2026).

But a complete profile is not the same thing as AI visibility.

For multi-location service brands, the better question is whether each Google Business Profile is backed by specific proof. A profile can say "AC repair," but the branch page should mention AC repair in that market, reviews should mention the service or city, and citations should point to the same branch and phone path.

Important

Use GBP to anchor identity. Use the location page, reviews, citations, and structured data to prove service, market, and contact facts.

![Image 2: Bar chart comparing business website and Google surface shares of pooled AI citations](https://www.cheers.tech/_next/image?url=%2Fimages%2Fgeo_academy_thumbnails%2Fis-google-business-profile-enough-for-ai-visibility.png&w=3840&q=75&dpl=dpl_BUHf3JVNo5aAPDqXGngMbjR3Ct5T)

Google Business Profile works best when the same local facts are confirmed by pages, reviews, and citations.

## Start with the profile, then verify the graph

Google Business Profile is not enough by itself. It is the owner-controlled place to maintain category, hours, address or service area, phone, services, photos, and reviews on Google surfaces. Google explicitly tells businesses to keep Business Profile information up to date for AI features in Search. Google also says AI Overviews and AI Mode rely on the same Search fundamentals: indexed pages, crawlable content, internal links, visible text, page experience, and structured data that matches the page.

Start with the fields that drift: primary category, additional categories, service area or address, hours, phone, services, website URL, photos, and review recency. Then check whether the linked page says the same thing. When service availability varies by branch, use [what services multi-location brands should list in Google Business Profile](https://www.cheers.tech/geo-academy/what-services-should-multi-location-brands-list-google-business-profile-ai-search) to keep the profile tied to real operations. For profile fields that change more often, add governance for [Google Business Profile Posts](https://www.cheers.tech/geo-academy/do-google-business-profile-posts-help-ai-search), [Google Business Profile Q&A](https://www.cheers.tech/geo-academy/google-business-profile-qa-ai-search), and [coupon or offer terms](https://www.cheers.tech/geo-academy/publish-coupons-offers-google-ai-search).

Some customer-facing facts do not fit cleanly inside profile fields. When they vary by branch, govern [response-time promises](https://www.cheers.tech/geo-academy/publish-response-times-ai-search), [accepted payment methods](https://www.cheers.tech/geo-academy/publish-payment-methods-ai-search), and [equipment-brand support](https://www.cheers.tech/geo-academy/publish-equipment-brands-ai-search) on the service or location page that can state the conditions, then keep the profile from contradicting that source.

Cheers' [Market Baseline](https://www.cheers.tech/research/ai-visibility-statistics) makes the gap measurable. Business websites supplied **68.1% of pooled citations**, while Google surfaces supplied **3.3%**, across 49,677 local-intent runs and 356,019 citations. That does not diminish the profile. It shows why the profile needs a strong owned source stack around it. Cheers Market Baseline, 28 days ending September 2, 2026, 100 metros, four engines, aggregate only. Read the [methodology](https://www.cheers.tech/research/methodology).

Once the profile is accurate, [the multi-location Business Profile performance guide](https://www.cheers.tech/geo-academy/google-business-profile-performance-metrics-multi-location) shows how to read discovery and action metrics without treating call clicks, website clicks, or directions as completed leads.

If your team needs the broader Google-specific guide, start with [How local businesses can show up in Google AI Search](https://www.cheers.tech/geo-academy/how-local-businesses-can-show-up-in-google-ai-search). For the product-level distinction between Gemini Apps, Ask Maps, Google AI Search, and Maps-grounded applications, use [How do I get my business recommended by Gemini?](https://www.cheers.tech/geo-academy/get-business-recommended-by-gemini). This article focuses on the profile question: what Google Business Profile can do, where it stops, and how multi-location operators should govern it.

## Why the profile still matters

Google says local results are mainly based on relevance, distance, and prominence. A complete Business Profile helps Google understand what the business does, where it operates, and when customers can reach it. Google also says review count and rating can factor into local ranking, while profile completeness, verification, hours, photos, and review responses all help customers evaluate the business.

For a service brand, those are not small details. They describe whether the location is a real match for the job.

An HVAC branch in Phoenix should not look identical to a plumbing branch in Dallas. A med spa franchise should not hide service differences behind one corporate profile template. A restoration company should not let one branch say "water damage restoration" on the profile while the matching location page only talks about the parent brand.

Google also explains that Business Profile information can come from business owners, publicly available web content, licensed third-party data, user contributions, reviews, photos, and Google's own interactions with the place. That is the point operators often miss. Google can reconcile owner fields with crawled pages, third-party data, user edits, reviews, and photos, so mismatches become profile ri

results.markdown:
Title: Managing Google Business Profiles for Multiple Locations: Centralized Control & SEO

URL Source: https://adwave.com/resources/managing-google-business-profiles-for-multiple-locations

Published Time: 2026-03-14T00:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
If you're managing more than a handful of business locations, you've probably realized that updating each Google Business Profile one by one is a recipe for disaster. A centralized system isn't a luxury; it's essential for keeping your brand consistent, your data accurate, and your sanity intact.

This approach saves an incredible amount of time and, more importantly, prevents the small, seemingly innocent errors that can seriously hurt your local search rankings.

## Build Your Foundation for Multi-Location Success

Juggling one Google Business Profile is work. Scaling that to dozens (or even hundreds) of locations is a completely different ballgame. The old way of manually changing holiday hours or posting a new promotion on each profile just doesn’t fly. For any multi-location brand serious about growth, moving to a centralized strategy is step one.

The absolute bedrock of this strategy is unwavering **NAP (Name, Address, Phone) consistency**. Think of your NAP data as the unique digital fingerprint for each location. When this information is perfectly identical everywhere (on your GBP listings, across local directories, and on your website) it sends a powerful trust signal to Google.

I've seen it countless times: a small inconsistency, like using "St." on one profile and "Street" on another, creates confusion for both search engines and customers. This splits your SEO authority and can lead people to the wrong place, or worse, to a competitor. For a deeper dive, check out our guide on why this matters so much: [https://adwave.com/resources/nap-consistency-why-your-business-name](https://adwave.com/resources/nap-consistency-why-your-business-name)

### The Power of a Unified System

To get this right across the board, you need a system. This means shifting from a location-by-location mindset to a portfolio-wide view. Getting organized from the start is the only way to prevent chaos down the road and ensure every single branch of your business reflects a strong, unified brand. Before you can optimize, you have to organize.

A key part of this organization is structuring your account with **location groups**. It’s like trying to manage 50 loose files on your desktop versus having them neatly sorted into labeled folders. Location groups bring that same order to your GBP account.

With location groups, you can:

*   Push essential updates (like a new company-wide service) to all listings at once.

*   Grant specific access to regional managers or franchise owners without giving away the keys to the whole kingdom.

*   Filter your performance data to compare how different regions or store types are doing.

> A study of **14,000** local business locations found that businesses using centralized tools to sync their listings saw a **28%** jump in 'Discovery' search views in just **90** days. When you consider that **46% of all Google searches have local intent**, that kind of visibility boost puts you right in front of customers in those critical "near me" moments.

Before we get into the nuts and bolts of daily management, let's look at the practical differences between the old way and the new.

### Single vs Multi-Location GBP Management Realities

This table breaks down the very different worlds of managing a single profile versus adopting a centralized, scalable strategy for many.

Seeing it laid out like this makes it clear: a manual approach just doesn't scale. A centralized system is the only way to maintain control and drive real results across an entire network of locations.

### Laying the Groundwork for Local SEO

All this foundational work is what makes your wider local SEO efforts possible. To make sure your multi-location strategy can succeed, you have to [build a rock-solid Google Business Profile foundation](https://growth4trades.com/how-to-rank-higher-on-google-maps/) for every single business. Each profile needs to be strong enough to rank on its own while contributing to the strength of the entire brand network.

This is where your marketing efforts connect. Imagine a potential customer sees a compelling ad from **Adwave** on their favorite streaming service. Their immediate reaction is to grab their phone and search "your brand near me."

A perfectly organized set of Google Business Profiles ensures the correct location pops up instantly. You capture that high-intent moment and turn brand awareness from the ad into a real visit or phone call. This initial setup is the launchpad for all your future multi-location marketing success.

## Mastering Bulk Setup and Verification

Adding a handful of new business locations to Google is a slog. But trying to add and verify dozens at once? That can feel like a one-way ticket to frustration, full of confusing rules and dead ends. The secret to managing this at scale is to forget the one-by-one method and lean into Google's bulk management tools.

At the heart of this whole process is a single, important document: the **bulk upload spreadsheet**. Your mission is to create a master file (a "single source of truth") that holds perfectly formatted data for every single one of your locations. Think of it as the architectural blueprint for your entire business network. Any mistake here will cause cracks in the foundation later.

### Getting Your Location Data Right the First Time

Before you even dream of uploading that spreadsheet, your data has to be immaculate. Google is notoriously finicky about formatting. A single misplaced comma or an inconsistent abbreviation (like "St." vs. "Street") can get your entire batch of locations rejected.

Start by downloading the official template from your Google Business Profile manager. Then, obsess over these columns:

*   **Store Code:** This is a unique ID _you_ create for each location. It must be unique and permanent, it's how Google and you will track that specific profile forever. Don't change it later.

*   **Business Name:** Make sure it's the real, public-facing name of your business. Resist the urge to add location-specific keywords like "Adwave - Downtown" unless that is the actual, registered name on your door.

*   **Address Lines:** Be meticulous. We're talking official street names, suite numbers, and postal codes. Consistency is absolutely everything.

*   **Primary Category:** Choose the **one best category** that describes what you do. This choice has a massive impact on the searches you show up for.

Once your sheet is filled out, go back and check every cell. Then, have someone else check it. It’s tedious, but it’s far less painful than untangling a dozen duplicate listings or failed verifications down the road.

> I’ve seen this go wrong too many times. For any business with over **10 locations**, designate a "data guardian." This person owns the master spreadsheet. Their job is to ensure every piece of information is 100% accurate and consistent _before_ anyone hits "upload."

### Your Verification Options at Scale

With your pristine data in hand, the next mountain to climb is verification. Having postcards mailed to dozens of locations is a logistical nightmare of lost mail and expiring codes. Fortunately, if you have **10 or more locations**, you're likely eligible for **bulk verification**.

This process lets you verify all your locations in one shot by proving to Google that you’re the legitimate operator of the brand. To get the ball rolling, you’ll first need to create a "location group" inside your GBP dashboard, which is essentially a folder for all your business profiles. Once you submit your spreadsheet, Google’s team will review your account and business to confirm you are who you say you are.

This diagram shows how to lay the groundwork for a solid multi-location structure before you even get to the verification step.

![Image 1: A three-step process flow diagram illustrating the GBP Foundation Process with NAP Consistency, Location Groups, and Unified Brand.](https://media.adwave.com/fia320z3blxi/1sr5HFs4k2LdE9pGPotm3K/ee710615f0954794823e21a4369eeffa/managing-google-business-profiles-for-multiple-locations-process-flow.jpg)
The key takeaway here is simple: consistent NAP (Name, Address, Phone) data and organized location groups are the non-negotiable first steps to presenting a unified, trustworthy brand.

### Troubleshooting Common Bulk Upload Headaches

Even with the best preparation, things can go sideways. The most common problems are flat-out rejected uploads or a verification process that seems stuck in limbo.

If Google flags errors in your spreadsheet, don't panic. It will usually provide a report showing the exact cells that need to be fixed. Correct them with surgical precision and re-upload the file.

Title: Create & manage posts on your Business Profile

URL Source: https://support.google.com/business/answer/7342169?hl=en

Markdown Content:
You can post updates on your Business Profile to share announcements, offers, updates, and event details directly with your customers on Search and Maps. When customers find your latest business updates on your Business Profile, it helps them decide to visit your business.

Post on your Business Profile to:

*   Share up-to-date info and improve your customer experience.
*   Promote your sales, specials, events, news, and offers.
*   Connect with your customers through posts with photos and videos.

[Understand where customers can find your posts](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7342169?hl=en)

Posts can show text, photos, or videos, and customers can find them in:

*   The “Updates” or “Overview” tabs of the Business Profile on mobile on Search and Maps.
*   The “From the owner” section of the Business Profile on your computer on Search and Maps.
*   Featured posts that are added directly to your Business Profile on mobile.

Posts about events, deals, or specials may automatically show on your Business Profile on mobile. These featured posts are from your social media channels, like Facebook and Instagram, or from posts you've created on your Business Profile.

**Tips:**

*   This feature is currently available in English for single-location food and drink businesses in the US, UK, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand.
*   When featured posts are available, customers find them in place of reviews on your Business Profile on mobile. They can still access reviews when they tap your business's star rating or check the "Reviews" tab.

[Understand the different types of posts](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7342169?hl=en)

**Important:** Posts that include a phone number in the post description might get rejected if they cannot be verified as being connected to the business on which they are posted. To add additional phone numbers to your profile, [learn more about edits to your Business Profile](https://support.google.com/business/answer/3039617#phone).

You can create and customize these types of posts:

*   **Updates:** Share info about your business. 
    *   You can add a description, photo, video, and an action button with a link. The button should direct customers to a website where they can complete the action, like make a booking, order online, or learn more.

*   **Offers:** Provide promotional sales or offers from your business. 
    *   It requires a title, dates, and time. This automatically includes a "View Offer" button on the post. You can also include a description, photo, video, coupon code, link, and terms and conditions. [Learn more about managing offers on your Business Profile](https://support.google.com/business/answer/18888417).

*   **Events:** Promote an event at your business. 
    *   Add a title, start and end dates, and times. If you don’t provide a start or end time, the event shows as lasting 24 hours on the event dates. You can also include a description, photo, video, and an action button.

**Tip:** Posts older than 6 months are archived unless a date range is set.

## [](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7342169?hl=en)Create a post

1.   [Go to your Business Profile](https://business.google.com/).
2.   Select **Posts**![Image 1: and then](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/3_l97rr0GvhSP2XV5OoCkV2ZDTIisAOczrSdzNCBxhIKWrjXjHucxNwocghoUa39gw=h36)**Add post**.
3.   Select the post type: 
    *   **Update**
    *   **Offer**
    *   **Event**

4.   Select the elements you want to add to your post. 
5.   Add info for your post. 
    *   If you want to schedule your post to publish at a later time, turn on **Schedule this post**, then select the date and time you want the post to publish.
    *   If you want to publish your post on a recurring basis, from the “Repeats” dropdown menu, select how often you want your post to show up, such as weekly, monthly, or a custom schedule.

6.   When you’re ready to publish, at the bottom right, select **Post**. 
    *   To post across multiple Business Profiles, select the profiles where you want to share it, then select **Post**.
    *   To share the post on one profile, select **Skip**.

**Tip:** To improve your posts, you can add details like a descriptive title, start and end date, and other relevant info. If details change, you can always edit a post to keep info up-to-date.

## Understand your post status

After you publish your post, Google reviews it to make sure it [meets our posts content policy](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7213077). Your post’s visibility to customers depends on its status:

*   **Live:** The post is public and shows on Search and Maps.
*   **Pending:** The post doesn't show on Search or Maps. It’s either in the upload stage, the processing stage, or your profile is unverified.
*   **Not approved:** The post doesn't show on Search or Maps. The question mark next to the status indicates which content policy the post violates.

## Tips to improve your posts

*   **Keep it professional:** Avoid misspelled words, extra characters, text that adds no value, and auto-generated or distracting content.
*   **Keep your posts respectful:** Do not use inappropriate or offensive language, images, or videos.
*   **Only post links to websites you trust:** The system doesn’t allow links that lead to malware, viruses, phishing, or pornographic material.
*   **Regulated goods and services:** You can use posts if you offer products or services in a regulated industry, but do not include content about the products. These industries usually include adult services, alcohol, tobacco, pharmaceutical products, recreational drugs, health and medical devices, gambling services, fireworks, weapons, and financial services.
*   **Keep your posts family-friendly:** Do not post sexually suggestive or explicit content.
*   **Add complete and relevant details:** Include a descriptive title, event start and end times, and offer info.
